summary: Defines the syntax of the Network Access Identifier (NAI), the user identity a client submits during network authentication, to support roaming between ISPs. It revises RFC 2486 with international character set and privacy support and corrections. It is on the standards track and was later replaced by RFC 7542.

plainLanguage.summary: A username written in a standard format that includes your home network, so a foreign network knows where to send your password check.

questions: what is a network access identifier
how long can an nai be
subtitle: The user@realm format that tells a roaming network where to send your login for checking.

tldr.problem: Roaming between ISPs needs a standard way to identify users, so a visiting network can find the user's home authentication server.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Access Identifier takes the form username@realm, where the realm is a DNS-style name. The RFC gives an ABNF grammar, length limits, username privacy rules, UTF-8 support and an optional syntax for routing through a mediating realm.
tldr.outcome: This revises RFC 2486 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 7542.

today: RFC 4282 is a Proposed Standard from December 2005. It obsoleted RFC 2486 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 7542.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
Roaming means using any one of several Internet Service Providers (ISPs) while keeping a formal customer relationship with only one. It covers dialup, VPN use, wireless LAN authentication and similar cases. The Network Access Identifier (NAI) is the user identity a client submits during network access authentication, and it also helps route the authentication request.

To offer roaming, the user's home authentication server has to be identifiable. The NAI sent to the Network Access Server (NAS) in the first authentication does that. NASes are also expected to use it when opening a tunnel, to find the tunnel endpoint. The NAI is not necessarily the same as the user's email address.
sections.plainLanguage: When you visit another network, it needs to know which home network to ask about you. The NAI is the name tag that says so.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
An NAI is a username, or @realm, or username@realm, defined in ABNF. The username is dot-separated strings of allowed characters, based on the grammar of RFC 821. Characters such as quotes, parentheses, comma, colon, semicolon, angle brackets and @ are not allowed unescaped, and a backslash can escape a character.

The realm is two or more labels separated by dots. A label starts with a letter or digit, so a realm can begin with a digit (such as 3com.com), which the DNS grammar of RFC 1035 did not permit. The RFC made this change to reflect current practice.

Devices MUST support an NAI length of at least 72 octets and SHOULD ideally support 253 octets. RADIUS cannot carry more than 253 octets and its RFC only recommends handling 63, while Diameter allows much longer values, so a long NAI may be cut off if it later passes through RADIUS.
sections.plainLanguage: An NAI looks like an email address: a name, an at sign and a network name. There are rules about which letters are allowed and how long it can be.

sections.title: Valid and Invalid Examples
sections.content:
The RFC lists valid NAIs such as bob, joe@example.com, fred.smith@example.com, @privatecorp.example.net and an internationalized realm written in ASCII form (alice@xn--tmonesimerkki-bfbb.example.net).

Invalid examples include fred@example (a realm needs at least two labels), fred@example_9.com, fred@example.net@example.net, fred.@example.net, and ones with :, ;, parentheses or angle brackets in the username.
sections.plainLanguage: Some names are fine, like joe@example.com. Others break the rules, like a name with two at signs.

sections.title: Username Privacy
sections.content:
The username part should be treated as opaque by nodes outside the realm's authoritative domain. When a separate authentication method can carry the username more securely, the NAI MAY be shortened by leaving out the username, as in @realm. The RFC recommends omitting it over using a fixed name such as anonymous, because omission clearly shows the name is not meant to identify one user.

The realm is normally still required, so the request can be routed to the right server. The security section adds that an NAI reveals the user's home affiliation, which can help an attacker probe the username space, so protocols can use transport protection such as RADIUS over IPsec or Diameter over TLS. Hiding the username protects it even from intermediate nodes such as NASes.
sections.plainLanguage: You can hide your own name on the badge and show only your home town. The network can still send the question to the right place without learning who you are.

sections.title: International Character Sets
sections.content:
Usernames may use Unicode encoded as UTF-8, so octets 128 to 255 are now allowed. Usernames MUST meet the requirements of RFC 4013 (SASLprep): mapping, normalization, checking for prohibited output, bidirectional handling and a ban on unassigned code points. End systems that take international text, typically the client and the AAA server, MUST do mapping, normalization and bidirectional processing, and MUST check for prohibited output and unassigned code points. NAIs travel on the wire in canonical form.

The realm is an IDN-unaware domain name slot, so it holds only ASCII. Conversion of internationalized names to ASCII is left to the end systems, and AAA routing uses the ASCII form.
sections.plainLanguage: Names can now use letters from many languages. The computers at each end tidy the name into one standard form, and the routers in the middle just pass it along.

sections.title: Realm Construction and Mediating Realms
sections.content:
Usually the home realm appears after the @, but sometimes the home realm can be reached only through another realm. An NAI MUST NOT name a different realm unless the sender knows that realm is available and supports this use, and using the home realm MUST be the default.

When allowed, user@homerealm.example.net MAY be written homerealm.example.net!user@otherrealm.example.net. The receiving realm MUST convert it back before passing it on, and the process can repeat for several hops. This syntax is optional and not part of the ABNF.

For naming, NAI realm names piggyback on DNS: the right to use a realm comes with the right to use the matching FQDN. Using an FQDN does not require using DNS to locate the authentication server, and an NAI need not be a valid email address.
sections.plainLanguage: If your home office can only be reached through another office, you can write the route on the badge. Each office along the way strips off its own part and passes it on.
